name: Yuan Dynasty
capital: Dadu (Khanbaliq, modern Beijing); summer capital Shangdu
summary: The Mongol-ruled dynasty founded by Kublai Khan, which ruled all of China from 1279 until it was driven north by the Ming in 1368.

knownFor.label: Paper money for the whole empire
knownFor.note: Marco Polo was amazed by it.

location.value: All of China plus Mongolia and Manchuria, ruled from Dadu (Khanbaliq, modern Beijing), with a summer capital at Shangdu. The nominal overlord of the other Mongol khanates.

terrain.value: The Mongolian steppe and the North China Plain, linked to the Yangtze region by an extended Grand Canal reaching Dadu.

climate.value: From the late 1340s, frequent droughts, floods and famines added to unrest.

resources.value: Southern rice and silk, northern pastoral wealth, and state monopolies on salt and iron.

disasters.value: Yellow River floods in the 1340s. In 1281 a typhoon (the “kamikaze”) destroyed the second invasion fleet sent against Japan.

population.value: About 87.6 million in 1351 (Wikipedia infobox estimate). Population had fallen sharply during the Mongol conquest, especially in the north.

urbanisation.value: Dadu was built as a new imperial capital from 1266. Hangzhou remained one of the richest cities in the world.

disease.value: Epidemics are reported in the 1330s–50s, but their link to the Black Death is debated.
disease.source: Brook, The Troubled Empire: China in the Yuan and Ming Dynasties (2010)

migration.value: Mongols and Central Asian (semuren) officials, merchants and soldiers moved into China. Western visitors included Marco Polo.

economicBase.value: Agriculture, crafts and trade, with heavy state monopolies (salt, iron) and merchant partnerships (ortogh) funding caravans.

tradeRoutes.value: The overland routes of the Mongol world, a protected postal relay system, and sea trade from Quanzhou. New crops arrived, including cotton and sorghum.

wealth.value: No GDP estimate is given in the sources checked.

moneyAndTax.value: Paper money (jiaochao) became the main currency. Over-issuing it caused severe inflation later in the dynasty. Wars and construction drained the treasury.

inequality.value: A legal hierarchy of four classes: Mongols, Central Asians (semuren), northern Chinese (Han), and southern Chinese (Nanren). The Han and southern populations were barred from owning weapons.

governmentType.value: An imperial monarchy under the Mongol Great Khan, using both Chinese institutions (Central Secretariat, Censorate) and Mongol ones.

keyRulers.value: Kublai Khan, grandson of Genghis Khan, who proclaimed the Yuan dynasty in 1271 (emperor from 1260, died 1294). Temür Khan (1294–1307). Toghon Temür (1332–1368, last to rule China). Chancellors Ahmad Fanakati and Toqto’a.
keyRulers.source: Wikipedia: Yuan dynasty (checked 5 Nov 2026) (infobox); video research: RESEARCH.md, “5,000 Years of China”

succession.value: No fixed rule. Successions were decided by assemblies (kurultai), and later by dowager empresses, guard units and powerful ministers. Nine emperors followed Kublai in 39 years.

institutions.value: Central Secretariat, Military Affairs Bureau, Censorate, and a bureau for Buddhist and Tibetan affairs. Civil service exams revived in 1313/1315 with quotas by class. The Da Yuan Tong Zhi law code.

stability.value: Civil war between Kublai and Ariq Böke (1260–64). Coups and the War of the Two Capitals (1328). The Red Turban Rebellion (1351–1368).

eliteConflict.value: Constant struggles among princes and chancellors (El Temür, Bayan, Toqto’a). The dismissal of Toqto’a in 1354 crippled the fight against the rebels.

armyAndTech.value: Mongol cavalry combined with Chinese infantry and navies (the “Han Army” and “Newly Submitted Army” of former Song troops). Siege engineers from Persia, and gunpowder weapons.

majorWars.value: Conquest of the Song (Xiangyang 1268–73, Yamen 1279). Failed invasions of Japan (1274, 1281). Defeat in Vietnam (Bạch Đằng, 1288). Campaigns in Burma, Champa and Java (1293).

territoryChange.value: About 11 million km² in 1310 (Wikipedia infobox). Lost China in 1368, but continued as the Northern Yuan in Mongolia.

alliancesRivals.value: Goryeo Korea was a close vassal. Rivals were the Chagatai and Ogedeid Mongols (Kaidu), Japan and Đại Việt. The western khanates recognised Yuan supremacy in 1304.

inventions.value: Guo Shoujing’s Shoushi calendar (1281), with a year of 365.2425 days. Wang Zhen’s agricultural treatise with wooden movable type (1313). Blue-and-white porcelain.

scienceEducation.value: Zhu Shijie’s algebra (Jade Mirror of the Four Unknowns, 1303). An Office of Western Medicine (1263) and Islamic astronomy at court.

openness.value: Highly open to foreign experts, merchants and religions across Eurasia, but the Chinese majority were excluded from top posts.

communicationTransport.value: The Mongol yam relay system across Asia, the Grand Canal (extended to Beijing) and paper money.

religion.value: Tibetan Buddhism was favoured at court. Taoism, Neo-Confucianism, Islam, and Nestorian and Catholic Christianity were tolerated, and Islam spread in the northwest and southwest.

languageWriting.value: Middle Mongol, Chinese (Old Mandarin) and Old Uyghur. The ʼPhags-pa script was made official for writing all of them.

artsArchitecture.value: The golden age of Chinese drama (zaju), vernacular writing, blue-and-white porcelain, and landscape painting by scholars who withdrew from office.

socialStructure.value: The four-class ethnic hierarchy, hereditary occupational households, and slaves taken in war.

sharedIdentity.value: Divided. Many Han Chinese did not see Mongol rule as legitimate, a feeling the Ming used in its rise. Calling the Yuan a “Chinese dynasty” is itself debated.

dailyLife.value: Chinese courtyard houses and Mongol tents; rice, millet, noodles, meat and milk.

neighbours.value: The Golden Horde, Chagatai Khanate and Ilkhanate, plus Goryeo, Japan, Đại Việt, Champa, Burma and Java.

ideasReligions.value: An era of Eurasian exchange (sometimes called the Pax Mongolica): Persian astronomy and medicine came in, and Chinese technology and paper money became known in the west.

colonisation.value: As conqueror, it ruled China and dominated neighbouring kingdoms as tributaries.

riseSignals.value: Built on the Mongol Empire’s conquests (Jin 1234). Kublai’s victory in the civil war (1264), adoption of Chinese institutions, and naval power for the Song conquest.

peakPeriod.value: The reign of Kublai Khan, after the Song conquest of 1279.

declineSignals.value: Succession struggles and coups, debt and inflation from paper money, corruption, ethnic discrimination, floods and famine in the 1340s, and the Red Turban Rebellion.

outcome.value: Driven out of China. The Ming took Dadu on 14 September 1368, and Toghon Temür fled north. The dynasty continued as the Northern Yuan in Mongolia.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Yuan dynasty (checked 5 Nov 2026); video research: RESEARCH.md, “5,000 Years of China”

sources.value: The History of Yuan (compiled quickly under the Ming), Persian sources (Rashid al-Din), Marco Polo, and Korean records. Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026. See also Rossabi (1988) and Brook (2010).

overallCertainty.value: Moderate. Dates vary by definition: start in 1260 (Kublai enthroned) or 1271 (name proclaimed), end in 1368 (loss of China) or later (Northern Yuan). The exam revival is dated 1313 or 1315.
